items.fullDescription: The erotic is a point of infinite signification, a navel in humanity’s symbolic circuit. However, despite its resistance to formalization, it is always in the process of not being written. As Octavio Paz insists, the erotic is a metaphor indelible to the human. As such, it is unsurprising that the manifestations of the erotic in subjective embodied experience are variable and correspond to equally plural treatments of it across the academic panorama. This diverse archive is bound by certain distinguishable threads, in terms of the potentiality of the erotic, its singular relation to language, and to the sphere of sexuality.

items.fullDescription: In January 2026, murals of faceless female silhouettes in yoga poses were scratched around the genital area in the Indian city of Gwalior. The figures depicted no identifiable women; they were attacked anyway. In 2024, sexually explicit AI-generated deepfakes of Taylor Swift circulated widely online, demonstrating a very different but related form of image violation. Across a scratched public wall and a fabricated digital image, the same question emerges: what happens when an image of a woman becomes the surface upon which sexualisation, humiliation or punishment is performed? This special issue asks where, if anywhere, a woman’s image can be assumed to be safe.

items.fullDescription: About the book: Human machine interfacing can be as simple as pressing a button or as complex and entangled (also entangling) as inserting a brain chip into the skull. science fiction. Humans with implants, prosthetic and hybrid humans with electronic and mechanical extensions are yet another level are no longer science fiction. items.fullDescription: At many universities, learning communities foster connectedness and belonging among students. Learning communities are typically composed of cohorts of students taking aligned first-year classes, but they take many other forms as well. At their best, they promote the perspective that learning is a collective activity in which knowledge is constructed through relationships with peers, professors, and communities, bringing together diverse voices and interdisciplinary perspectives. They provide a welcoming environment that eases the transition to college and provides a foundation for a peer network of academic support (Schreiber & Valle, 2013).

items.fullDescription: Over the past three decades, fan studies have developed sophisticated accounts of participatory culture, collective intelligence, affective engagement, and transformative practices (Jenkins 2006; Booth 2015; Hills 2017). At the same time, scholarship has increasingly addressed the investigative dimensions of audience participation. Mittell’s concept of “forensic fandom” (2009), for example, highlights practices of close reading, clue collection, speculation, and collaborative interpretation in response to complex narrative worlds. Fans thus become active investigators who uncover hidden meanings, solve mysteries, and assemble fragmented information across media texts. More recently, such investigative practices have expanded beyond fictional worlds.

items.fullDescription: How is everyone doing? At a routine meeting of the Editorial Board of this journal in March 2026, this innocuous question erupted into disquiet, tension, unease. Speaking from vastly different parts of the world, there was an unmistakable sense of a planet slipping beyond available comprehension and unplugging us from work and life routines. As wars in the Middle East expand and fires spread from apartment blocks reduced to rubble to bombed oil refineries and shipping corridors, profound geopolitical, personal, even psychic rifts leave us grasping for the language and feel of the moment, the falling apart of things, the zeitgeist of an endangered now.

items.fullDescription: Over recent decades, decadence studies has moved beyond earlier identifications of decadence with the Western European literary and artistic canon of the fin de siècle . Recent scholarship has, for example, developed new critical approaches to decadence, from translation studies to affect and sensory studies to postcolonial theory; illuminated the global dimensions of decadence; traced its afterlives and new literary histories; and examined its significance across diverse artistic and sociocultural practices, from food and fashion to performance and popular media. Taken together, these efforts underline the continued resonance of decadence as a capacious and multifaceted phenomenon for thinking about the many faces of modernity.

items.fullDescription: Bringing affect theory back to its seventeenth-century literary and cultural contexts, this conference seeks to explore how this period’s literature represents different affects; how reader responses are shaped by affect; and how both these negotiations reflect broader social or scientific developments of the period. A critical focus on affect can offer insights into the entanglement of body and mind, the sensible and the imagined, aesthetic practice, as well as the contexts and environments in which bodies move and interact. In the broadest sense, textual negotiations of affect point to what is at stake in reading.

items.fullDescription: Every act of communication, interpretation, and representation is an act of framing. In literary analysis, a “frame” might define genre, direct narrative perspective, or position a text within a historical moment. In linguistics, frames organize semantic understanding, govern pragmatic interaction, and underpin metaphor. In translation and interpreting, frames are negotiated, shifted, and sometimes shattered in the movement between languages and cultures. They are the selective filters that highlight certain elements while relegating others to the background, the conceptual structures that allow us to categorize, interpret, and communicate complex realities.

items.fullDescription: In 2007, Director Anne Lewis documented Hispanic/Latinx Appalachian "workers who speak about their lives, work, disappointments, and hope." Since that time, a significant boom of Hispanic/Latinx individuals has gained further recognition in Appalachian culture and community. Bands such as Appalatin and Che Apalache have been formed, academic papers have been written on migration patterns and demographic analysis, and oral history narratives have been collected. The very presence of these individuals has been established in the physical, factual realm of nonfiction spaces. However, very little has been explored in terms of Hispanic Appalachian fiction.

items.fullDescription: Special Issue Rationale Artificial intelligence has arrived in education with the force of a paradigm shift. Adaptive tutors, generative writing assistants, automated assessment, personalized learning pathways -- the claims are sweeping and the investments enormous. Education ministries, platform companies, and philanthropic foundations are converging on a single proposition: AI will transform how human beings learn. What remains largely unasked is whether this transformation is sustainable , and what, precisely, we mean by that word when we apply it to learning itself.
